questions.q: What is the core difference between human rights and fundamental rights in terms of their scope and enforceability?
questions.a: Human rights are universal (apply to all humans globally) and derive from international law (UDHR, treaties), while fundamental rights are country-specific (e.g., only in India under Part III) and enforceable in domestic courts. A wrong answer confusing them as identical reveals the student hasn't grasped that human rights are *moral/legal claims on all states*, whereas fundamental rights are *constitutional guarantees by a specific state*.

questions.q: Explain why the "Golden Triangle" (Articles 14, 19, 21) is called so, using the *Maneka Gandhi* case as illustration.
questions.a: The Golden Triangle means Articles 14 (equality), 19 (freedoms), and 21 (life/liberty) are interdependent — a law depriving liberty (Art. 21) must also satisfy equality (Art. 14) and reasonableness under freedoms (Art. 19). In *Maneka Gandhi*, passport impoundment violated Art. 21, but the Court held it must also meet Art. 14 (non-arbitrariness) and Art. 19 (freedom of movement). A wrong answer treating them as isolated rights shows failure to understand the *integrated due process* standard established post-1978.

questions.q: A foreign tourist in India is denied entry to a public park based on nationality. Which rights are violated — human rights, fundamental rights, or both? Justify.
questions.a: Both. Human rights (UDHR Art. 2: non-discrimination) are violated because they apply to *all humans*. Fundamental rights (Art. 15: prohibition of discrimination on grounds including place of birth) are also violated — though Art. 15 says "citizen," Art. 14 ("any person") and Art. 21 ("no person") extend protection to non-citizens for equality and life/liberty. A wrong answer saying "only human rights" misses that the Indian Constitution protects *persons*, not just citizens, for core rights.

questions.q: Compare the enforceability of Directive Principles (Part IV) vs. Fundamental Rights (Part III) in Indian courts, and explain how the Supreme Court bridged this gap using Article 21.
questions.a: Fundamental Rights are justiciable (enforceable in courts); Directive Principles are non-justiciable (Art. 37). The Court bridged this by reading Directive Principles (e.g., Art. 39A — free legal aid, Art. 41 — right to work) *into* Article 21 (right to life), making them enforceable. Example: *Olga Tellis* read "right to livelihood" (Directive Principle) into Art. 21. A wrong answer stating Directive Principles are "never enforceable" ignores this judicial innovation.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is legally binding on all UN member states, including India."
questions.a: The statement is false. UDHR is a General Assembly *resolution* (soft law), not a treaty — it creates moral/political obligations, not legal bindingness. Binding obligations come from *ratified treaties* like ICCPR and ICESCR (which India ratified in 1979). A wrong answer calling UDHR "binding" confuses aspirational declarations with treaty law — a critical distinction in international law.

questions.q: Design a hypothetical scenario where a state law violates the "basic structure" doctrine by undermining human rights, and explain which component of basic structure it attacks.
questions.a: Scenario: A law removes judicial review of detention orders under preventive detention, allowing executive to detain indefinitely without court scrutiny. This attacks "judicial review" and "rule of law" — both basic structure components (*Kesavananda Bharati*, *Minerva Mills*). A good answer identifies the specific basic structure feature (not just "fundamental rights") and explains *why* its removal destroys constitutional identity. A poor answer vaguely says "it violates rights" without naming the structural pillar.
